item.title: Depth of leaves in closed linear $\lambda$-terms: exact recurrence, limit law and edge window
item.description: arXiv:2611.31323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $K_n$ (resp.\ $D_n$) be the depth of a uniform leaf (resp.\ node) in a uniform closed linear $\lambda$-term of size $n$. A bijective \emph{grafting identity} yields an exact polynomial-time recurrence for the full depth profile. By the method of moments, $K_n/n$ converges in law to the density $3x/\sqrt{1-2x}$ on $[0,\frac12]$, i.e.\ $2K_n/n\to\Beta(2,\frac12)$, with $\mathbb E[K_n^r]/n^r\to3(r+1)!/(2r+3)!!$; likewise $1-2D_n/n\to\Beta(\frac12,1)$. A backward Markov chain gives the corresponding local limits for $k\le(\frac12-\varepsilon)n$. The limit density diverges at $\frac12$, and the profile has a second scale: a window of width $\sqrt n$ around $n/2$, which carries a fraction of order $n^{-1/4}$ of the nodes, at a density $n^{1/4}$ times larger than in the bulk. We prove that a single explicit function describes both regimes: uniformly in $d$, \[ n^{3/4}\,\mathbb P(D_n=d)=g\Bigl(\tfrac{d-n/2}{\sqrt n}\Bigr)+O(n^{-1/16}),\qquad n^{3/4}\,\mathbb P(K_n=d)=\tfrac{3d}{n}\,g\Bigl(\tfrac{d-n/2}{\sqrt n}\Bigr)+O(n^{-1/16}), \] where $g(y)=2^{-1/2}e^{-y^2}D_{-1/2}(2y)$ is a parabolic cylinder function. In particular $\mathbb P(K_n>n/2)\sim\frac34\,\mathbb E|Z|^{1/2}\,n^{-1/4}\approx0.6166\,n^{-1/4}$ with $Z$ standard Gaussian. The proofs rest on harmonic functions of the heat equation evaluated along the backward chain.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Bodini (LAGA)

item.title: CrossCheck I: Cost Bounds of Imperative Programs as Constrained Optimization, with a Sound Cost Logic and a Verified Certificate Checker
item.description: arXiv:2611.31430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Static analysis of imperative programs often relies on iterative fixed-point approximations or concrete path exploration. We show that structured imperative control flow---while loops, linear recursion and branching recursion---can be mapped into constrained optimization problems over the free monoid of execution traces and the free algebra of computation trees. Ordering traces and trees by an intensional \textit{order-by-composition} ($\sqsubseteq$), halting is characterized as finding the minimal trace or tree that satisfies the exit condition, and we prove that this characterization coincides with the standard big-step semantics. Exact state recurrences are undecidable in general, so we relax them into cost envelopes, using ranking potentials and the tropical $(\max,+)$ reading of the timing schema, and obtain sound upper bounds on execution cost. The bounds compose over whole programs in a cost logic for a small language with nondeterministic actions, procedures, recursion and assumed contracts, which we prove sound for terminating and non-terminating executions. A linear instance of the logic has certificates---programs annotated with invariants, potentials and Farkas multipliers---and a checker that validates them with integer arithmetic only; an accepted certificate bounds the cost of every execution. All results, the checker and the worked examples are machine-checked in Lean~4. A companion paper describes a Clang plugin that produces such certificates and its evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Luca Dall'Olio

item.title: CrossCheck II: A Compiler Plugin for Certified Cost Bounds of Real-Time C and C++ Code, and its Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.31449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We describe a plugin for the Clang compiler that bounds the cost of C and C++ functions intended for real-time use, and rejects at compile time the functions that allocate, throw, call through pointers, or contain a loop or a recursion for which no bound is found. Loops are bounded by affine ranking potentials synthesized with an SMT solver through Farkas' Lemma, or by logarithmic ones, recursion by depth and size potentials, and callees are analyzed in the calling context in which they are used. For functions in a linear fragment, the plugin emits a cost certificate that a checker, compiled from a Lean~4 definition proved sound in a companion paper, validates with integer arithmetic only; the bound then depends neither on the analyzer nor on the solver. On the 29 kernels of the TACLeBench collection, without annotations, the plugin bounds 142 of 220 loops in the calling contexts of the programs, 131 of them exactly as the benchmarks' flow facts, and 161 of the 165 bounded functions receive a certificate that the checker accepts, 152 of them also validated against an independent description of the source. On the CMSIS-DSP library for Cortex-M (786 functions), with assumed input ranges, it bounds 616 functions. We compare the loop bounds with loop counts observed by running the kernels and with five existing analyzers (LLVM's ScalarEvolution, KoAT2, CoFloCo, Infer and oRange), and the plugin with KoAT2 and CoFloCo on the C programs of the Termination and Complexity Competition: without annotations, 147 of 553 programs receive a certified bound that holds for all inputs, where the two tools bound 288 and 264. Loop bounds, exported annotations and the checker program are also tested on random programs and on mutated certificates.
item.dc:creator: Luca Dall'Olio

item.title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
item.description: arXiv:2611.31811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.
item.dc:creator: Nikolaos Nikolaou

item.title: Self-Reference and Relative Incompleteness: From Logical Obstructions to Hardness Hypotheses
item.description: arXiv:2611.32095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define relative incompleteness and use it to provide a unified framework for G\"odelian incompleteness and the limits of local observations in finite SAT. A background is incomplete relative to a target question if two realizations compatible with that background give opposite answers. G\"odelian diagonalization yields a sentence whose truth value differs across two models of the same theory, while solution-dependent blocking yields two formulas that agree on the observed clauses but differ in satisfiability. Both constructions realize a common diagonal relation between truth and acceptance that forces a sound partial evaluator to leave the target undecided. For a satisfiable formula, replacing a single unobserved clause without changing its variable support can make the formula unsatisfiable exactly when all solutions remaining after deletion of that clause agree on its support. If the original formula has a unique solution, this condition is equivalent to redundancy of the clause. More generally, an observation of a satisfiable formula determines satisfiability exactly when it includes a position at which the formula differs from each unsatisfiable completion. For uniquely satisfiable formulas, the positions that every sufficient observation must include are precisely the redundant ones. We also arithmetize solution blocking and construct a tagged fixed point that refers to its own blocking data. Finally, we use self-referential $K$-SAT to illustrate how relative incompleteness can provide a logical foundation for formulating a quantitative hardness hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Jie Luo, Ke Xu

item.title: SAT Solving for Power Peak Minimization in the Parallel--Serial--with--Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.32141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Parallel--Serial-with-Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem with Power Peak Minimization (PSCALB3PM) was introduced by Delorme and Gianessi (2022), who proposed an integer linear programming (ILP) model, and further developed in 2024 with a multi-start local-search matheuristic. This paper presents an exact approach based on Boolean satisfiability (SAT) that combines a compact encoding with incremental SAT solving. Specifically, it develops a compact encoding of task-to-workstation precedence constraints and an incremental SAT-based optimization procedure for power peak minimization. We evaluate the proposed method on 375 benchmark instances and compare it with both reference methods. SAT finds feasible solutions for all 375 instances and certifies optimality for 159, compared with 346 feasible solutions and 126 optimality certificates obtained by the ILP method. Relative to the reference matheuristic, SAT achieves lower power peaks on 130 instances, whereas the matheuristic obtains lower values on only four. These findings establish SAT as a competitive exact method for PSCALB3PM, achieving higher feasible-solution coverage and more optimality proofs than the reference ILP model, while generally outperforming the existing matheuristic in terms of solution quality.
item.dc:creator: Chi Phong Nguyen, Khanh Van To

item.title: Concurrent Visibility: Higher-Order Concurrency with First-Order Store
item.description: arXiv:2611.32234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an Operational Game Semantics for a (call-by-value) concurrent higher-order language with first-order store (references may contain other references or first-order values such as integers or booleans; however they may not store higher-order values such as functions). We adapt the game-semantic notion of visibility, which semantically captures the absence of higher-order references and developed for sequential higher-order languages, to a concurrent setting. We thus define a complete-trace preorder, and prove it sound for the contextual preorder, by introducing a synchronization-based composition of semantic configurations and establishing an observational adequacy result. We also prove completeness for the subset of the language in which functions return first-order values. In contrast to the case of sequential visibility, in the labeled transition semantics we have to account for the presence of multiple active threads with possibly different visibilities, and of a tree-like structure for managing the dependencies among the threads so created. Moreover, we have to reason on families of traces, rather than single traces, as in concurrent setting the order among certain actions cannot be enforced.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 37th International Conference on Concurrency Theory, CONCUR 2026, Ana Sokolova and Patrick Totzke, Sep 2026, Liverpool, United Kingdom. pp.45:1--45:20

item.title: On Presburger Arithmetic Expanded with Prime Numbers
item.description: arXiv:2611.32977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove unconditionally that the first-order theory of Presburger arithmetic expanded by a predicate for the primes is undecidable. Bateman, Jockusch and Woods proved this in 1993 assuming Dickson's conjecture. We use the counter-machine framework of Karimov, Nieuwveld and Ouaknine and their idea of using `arbitrary permutations', and the number-theoretic input comes from Hildebrand and Maier's 1988 proof that the limit points of $k$ consecutive normalised prime gaps have positive measure. We use a discrete version, which they obtain before limits are taken. The key lemma is that although Hildebrand and Maier's result does not seem to give arbitrary permutations of consecutive prime gaps, it gives arbitrary permutations for the differences $p_i - q_i$ for two finite blocks of consecutive primes $p_0 < \cdots < p_k$ and $q_0 < \cdots < q_k$. Moreover, with the same key lemma, we show that Presburger arithmetic expanded with the function that maps $n$ to the $n$th prime defines multiplication.
item.dc:creator: Joris Nieuwveld

item.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
item.description: arXiv:2611.31286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts. The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.
item.dc:creator: Richard DeMillo, Richard Lipton

item.title: Symbolic Proof Compression and Fractal Universality: A Conditional Non-Constructive Refutation of the Riemann Hypothesis
item.description: arXiv:2611.31469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Building on S.~C.~Woon's (1994) fractal and symbolic reformulation of Voronin's Universality Theorem, we construct a formal, non-constructive proof-by-contradiction architecture exploring the Riemann Hypothesis ($\mathsf{RH}$). Woon's Corollary~3 permits arbitrary finite binary strings to be encoded into nowhere-vanishing exponential waveforms on a closed disk inside the critical strip. Combining effective upper bounds for Voronin universality (Good, Garunk\v{s}tis) with Cauchy-integral Taylor decoding yields an explicit finite rational grid $\mathcal{G}_{L_0}$ below an effective ceiling $H_{\mathrm{crit}}(L_0)$ within which every formal proof of bit-length at most $L_0$ is imprinted with zero flipped digits. We introduce a conjectural \emph{Zeta-Universal Symbolic Proof Compression Hypothesis} ($\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$), positing that the global regularity implied by $\mathsf{RH}$ compresses true $\Pi_1^0$ statements about $\zeta(s)$ into $\mathsf{ZFC}$ derivations of bounded length $L_0$. Assuming classical logic and $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$, G\"odel--Carnap diagonalization over bounded zeta-encoded provability yields a contradiction. The self-referential result converts a digital encoding framework with any uniform proof-compression principle for RH into an immediate non-constructive refutation of RH. Given that, with human input and computer assistance, $\mathsf{RH}$ has been formally verified in the Lean theorem prover strictly within constructive logic, this contradiction does not refute $\mathsf{RH}$. Instead, it falsifies $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$. We conclude by isolating the exact proof-theoretic obstruction---Pudl\'ak's lower bound on bounded reflection proofs---showing why the analytic regularity of $\mathsf{RH}$ cannot compress logical self-reference, and exposing the limits of applying the Law of Excluded Middle to uncomputably bounded searches.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Martin Lisewski

item.title: Safe Autoformalization: Sufficiency and Necessity with Entailment Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.31571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autoformalization translates a natural-language statement into a formula that captures its intent, which depends on the statement's context: the background that disambiguates it. LLMs make autoformalization practical, but their probabilistic output carries no formal guarantees. We propose techniques for safe autoformalization that certify one-sided logical adequacy: a formula sufficient for the intent is safe to enforce, and a formula necessary for it is safe to rely on. We use LLMs to generate candidate formulas and order them by logical strength in an Entailment Graph (EG), an ordering a solver decides. Each edge carries a residual and a co-residual, the two adjoints of the entailment order, all fixed by the candidate pool alone. In a context, two searches return the sufficient frontier, the weakest candidates that entail the statement, and the necessary frontier, the strongest candidates the statement entails; each step is one local check against an edge's residual or co-residual. The frontiers bracket the statement and yield the ambiguity residue, which holds exactly of the situations the candidates certify neither as satisfying nor as violating it; the statement is ambiguous precisely when the residue is satisfiable. For natural-language statements and contexts, an LLM entailment oracle decides the checks; it is sound if it accepts only checks that hold, and complete if it accepts every check that holds. We prove that a sound oracle makes the search safe regardless of pool quality, and that a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, EGs are safe in all 20 cases of an expert-adjudicated study, where majority vote over equivalence clusters and Universal Self-Consistency are unsafe in 25% and 10%. An ablation with the same oracle but no graph is unsafe in 25% and rejects every candidate in another 30%. We machine-checked our proofs in Lean.
item.dc:creator: Umut A. Acar, Eli Goldweber

item.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.32868v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.
item.dc:creator: Nikolaos Kekatos, Antonio Anastasio Bruto da Costa, Alexios Lekidis, Pabitra Mitra, Hosein Nazarpour, Priyanka Sinha

item.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33078v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.
item.dc:creator: Yisrael Clark, Guy Katz

item.title: Elementary first-order model checking for sparse graphs
item.description: arXiv:2401.16230v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is known that for subgraph-closed graph classes the first-order model checking problem is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if the class is nowhere dense [Grohe, Kreutzer, Siebertz, 2017]. However, the dependency on the formula size is non-elementary, and in fact, this is unavoidable even for the class of all trees [Frick and Grohe, 2004]. On the other hand, it is known that the dependency is elementary for classes of bounded degree [Frick and Grohe, 2004] as well as for classes of bounded pathwidth [Lampis, 2026]. In this paper we generalise these results and almost completely characterise subgraph-closed graph classes for which the model checking problem is fixed-parameter tractable with an elementary dependency on the formula size. Those are the graph classes for which there exists a number $d$ such that for every $r$, some tree of depth $d$ and size bounded by an elementary function of $r$ is avoided as an $(\le r)$-subdivision in all graphs in the class. In particular, this implies that if the class in question excludes a fixed tree as a topological minor, then first-order model checking for graphs in the class is fixed-parameter tractable with an elementary dependency on the formula size.
item.dc:creator: Jakub Gajarsk\'y, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk, Marek Soko{\l}owski, Giannos Stamoulis, Szymon Toru\'nczyk

item.title: Counting on Nowhere Dense Classes
item.description: arXiv:2609.18875v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish an algorithmic framework for query answering and enumeration in first-order logic with counting on effectively nowhere dense classes of relational structures. Our main technical contribution is an algorithm that, after almost-linear-time preprocessing on a structure $A$ from such a class and a first-order formula $\phi(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, can answer the following queries in constant time: given a tuple $\bar{v} \in A^{|\bar{x}|}$, output the number of tuples $\bar{w} \in A^{|\bar{y}|}$ satisfying $A \models \phi(\bar{v},\bar{w})$. In database terms, this is constant-time evaluation of grouped counting queries. Building on this, we achieve constant-time query answering and constant-delay enumeration for the recently introduced clique-guarded first-order logic with counting (cgFOC) [van Bergerem, Lange, and Schweikardt, MFCS 2026] on effectively nowhere dense classes. These results unify and generalise previous work on nowhere dense classes, namely first-order testing and enumeration [Schweikardt, Segoufin, and Vigny, JACM 2022] and the evaluation of the counting logic FOC1 [Grohe and Schweikardt, PODS 2018]. Moreover, under the assumption $\mathrm{FPT} \neq \mathrm{AW}[*]$, our results are essentially optimal: they do not extend to subgraph-closed graph classes beyond the nowhere dense ones, slight generalisations of the clique-guarding mechanism are intractable even on very simple sparse classes, and very restricted fragments of cgFOC are already intractable on very simple dense classes.
item.dc:creator: Steffen van Bergerem, Nicole Schweikardt

item.title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
item.description: arXiv:2610.35523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but synthesizing them remains challenging and often requires substantial expertise. Despite considerable progress in their automated synthesis, existing approaches remain limited in their effectiveness. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that tightly integrates large language models (LLMs) with symbolic verification. To our best knowledge, RAINFALL is the first to employ a generate-verify-refine paradigm for LLM-based ranking function synthesis. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the input program that the LLM must fill in four predefined slots per loop. The resulting program is checked by a symbolic verifier. Successful verification yields a valid ranking function, while verification failures produce diagnostics that are translated into natural-language feedback to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, RAINFALL synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 programs (93.02%), outperforming all evaluated baselines. Notably, it solves 22 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. Combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 further increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). Ablation studies demonstrate the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback, while experiments across different LLMs establish the broader applicability of the framework.
item.dc:creator: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu, Qiusong Yang

item.title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)
item.description: arXiv:2611.18541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $\Theta_0, \Theta_1, \Theta_2, \dots$ with $\Theta_k \circ \Theta_j = \Theta_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $\Theta_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two. Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.
item.dc:creator: William DeMeo, Ralph Freese

item.title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^2$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.27814v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $\epsilon >0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{2-\epsilon})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{2k-\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the input size. Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.
item.dc:creator: A. R. Balasubramanian, Rupak Majumdar
